passages.title: One Night Without Streetlights
passages.passage:
Every year on the last Saturday of October, the small coastal town of Cửa Đông does something that surprises visitors. At nine o'clock in the evening, the street lamps along the harbour go out, the cafés turn off their coloured signs, and families carry blankets down to the beach. For two hours, the only light comes from the sky.

The event, called Dark Sky Night, was started six years ago by Mr Hải, a retired ship's engineer. As a young sailor, he had learned to find his way by the stars, and he was sad that his grandchildren had never seen the Milky Way. "They could name every planet from their textbook," he says, "but they thought the sky above our town was empty." He asked the town council to switch off the lights for one evening. To his surprise, they agreed, on the condition that it did not cost anything.

The first year, about forty people came. Mr Hải borrowed a telescope from a secondary school and pointed out Saturn, whose rings made several children shout. Since then, the crowd has grown to over a thousand, and local teachers now prepare star maps that visitors can read with a red torch, which does not spoil night vision the way white light does.

Not everyone was happy at first. Some shop owners feared losing customers, and a few residents felt unsafe walking home in the dark. The council answered by keeping the lights on in the side streets and asking volunteers to guide people along the beach path.

For Mr Hải, the best moment comes each year just after the lamps go off. "There is always a silence," he says, "and then someone gasps. That is the sound of a person seeing the sky properly for the first time." He hopes that one day the town will use dimmer lamps all year round, so that the stars are not only a once-a-year event.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: The dangers of walking home in the dark in a coastal town
Why children can name the planets but never look at the sky
How a retired sailor learned to navigate by the stars
A yearly event in which a town turns off its lights to see the stars
questions.explanation: Every paragraph is about Dark Sky Night: how it began, how it grew, the problems it caused and what it means to Mr Hải. His years as a sailor and the safety worries are details inside that story.

questions.q: On what condition did the town council agree to Mr Hải's request?
options: That shop owners along the harbour supported the idea
That the event would attract visitors to the town
That the event would not cost the town any money
That Mr Hải would provide a telescope himself
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the council agreed on the condition that it did not cost anything. The telescope was borrowed, and the shop owners were actually against the idea at first.

questions.q: Why do visitors read the star maps with a red torch?
options: Because white light is banned in the town on that evening
Because red light does not damage people's night vision
Because red torches are cheaper for the school to buy
So that the volunteers can see where the visitors are
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 explains that a red torch does not spoil night vision the way white light does. Nothing is said about a ban, the price of torches or the volunteers.

questions.q: What can be inferred about how the council dealt with the complaints?
options: It found a compromise instead of stopping the event
It told the shop owners to close early on Dark Sky Night
It refused to listen to the residents who felt unsafe
It cancelled the event for one year while it found a solution
questions.explanation: The council kept the lights on in the side streets and provided volunteer guides, which answered the safety worries without ending the event. That is a compromise, not a cancellation or a refusal.

questions.q: The word "gasps" in the last paragraph is closest in meaning to:
options: begins to cry quietly
shouts a person's name
laughs loudly
takes a sudden breath in surprise
questions.explanation: Mr Hải describes a silence followed by the sound of someone seeing the sky properly for the first time. A gasp is the short, sudden breath a person takes when amazed.

questions.q: In paragraph 2, "they agreed" refers to:
options: the visitors to the town
the shop owners
the town council
Mr Hải's grandchildren
questions.explanation: The sentence before says Mr Hải asked the town council to switch off the lights, so "they" is the council that agreed to his request.

questions.q: Mr Hải owned the telescope that was used on the first Dark Sky Night.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says he borrowed the telescope from a secondary school, so the statement contradicts the passage.

passages.title: A Museum Without Glass Cases
passages.topic: a class trip to a museum
passages.passage:
Last Friday, Class 9A2 at Nguyễn Trãi Secondary School spent the day at the Museum of Traditional Crafts on the edge of the city. Most of the students expected a quiet morning of walking past glass cases and reading small labels. What they found was quite different.

The museum opened two years ago in a former rice warehouse. Instead of keeping objects behind glass, it invites visitors to touch, lift and even use them. In the first room, a guide named Ms Lan handed each student a piece of wet clay and showed them how a village potter shapes a bowl on a turning wheel. "Half of them made something that looked like a hat," she laughed, "but they will remember how hard it is."

The trip had been planned by the class's history teacher, Mr Dũng, who wanted his students to understand a chapter about village trades that they had found dull in the textbook. He asked them to choose one craft during the visit and interview a museum worker about it. Later, each group would present what they had learned to the rest of the class.

For Phương, a student who admits she nearly stayed at home with a cold, the highlight was the weaving room. An elderly woman there had been making silk for fifty years, and she let Phương try the loom. "I thought weaving was slow and boring," Phương said. "After ten minutes my arms hurt and I had made about three centimetres of cloth. Now I understand why silk was so expensive."

The day was not perfect. The bus arrived forty minutes late, and the museum café ran out of food before the last group had eaten. Even so, when Mr Dũng asked whether the class would like to visit again, every hand went up. He plans to make the trip a yearly event, and the museum has offered a discount for future school groups.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Why school trips are often badly organised
How silk was made in Vietnamese villages in the past
A class visit to a museum where visitors can handle the objects
The history of a rice warehouse that became a museum
questions.explanation: The passage follows Class 9A2 through the visit, what they did there and how they felt about it. The warehouse, the silk and the late bus are single details within that account.

questions.q: Why did Mr Dũng organise the trip?
options: Because he wanted the class to practise interviewing people
Because the museum had offered his class a discount
Because his students had asked to go somewhere outside school
Because his students had found a textbook chapter boring
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says he wanted the students to understand a chapter about village trades that they had found dull. The interviews were a task during the trip, and the discount was offered only after the visit.

questions.q: What does Ms Lan's comment about the "hat" suggest?
options: Most of the students found the pottery difficult
The students were not listening to her instructions
She was disappointed with the class's behaviour
The students had been asked to make hats, not bowls
questions.explanation: She laughs that half of the bowls looked like hats and adds that the students will remember how hard it is. Her point is that shaping clay is harder than it looks, not that the class misbehaved.

questions.q: The word "highlight" in paragraph 4 is closest in meaning to:
options: the most difficult task
the best part
the final activity
the brightest room
questions.explanation: Phương goes on to describe the weaving room as the experience that changed her mind, so "highlight" means the most enjoyable or memorable part of the day.

questions.q: Why does the writer mention the late bus and the café running out of food?
options: To prove that the trip had been planned too quickly
To criticise the museum for being poorly managed
To show that the day had problems but the students still enjoyed it
To explain why the students want to visit the museum again
questions.explanation: The paragraph begins "The day was not perfect" and continues with Even so, every hand went up. The problems are mentioned to make the students' enthusiasm more convincing.

questions.q: Phương had visited the Museum of Traditional Crafts before this trip.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: The passage says Phương nearly stayed at home with a cold and describes her first try at the loom, but it never says whether she had been to the museum before.

questions.q: The museum is in a building that was once used to store rice.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 states that the museum opened in a former rice warehouse, which is a building where rice was stored.

passages.title: Twelve Floors Up
passages.passage:
When Bảo's family moved into a flat on the twelfth floor of a new building, his mother made one condition: she wanted to grow her own vegetables. Bảo's father pointed out that they no longer had a garden, only a narrow balcony that got sun for a few hours each morning. His mother simply replied that she would start small.

She began with three plastic boxes filled with soil from a market stall. In the first one she planted water spinach, which she said was almost impossible to kill. In the second she sowed lettuce, and in the third some chilli seeds she had saved from the kitchen. Bảo was given the job of watering them before school, and he expected to forget within a week.

To his surprise, the water spinach was ready to cut after three weeks. His mother stir-fried it with garlic, and the whole family agreed that it tasted sweeter than anything from the supermarket. The lettuce was a different story. Snails climbed up from the drain and ate most of it, and the leaves that survived turned bitter in the afternoon heat. "Every garden teaches you something," his mother said, and moved the box into the shade.

By the end of the year, the balcony held eleven boxes, two hanging pots of mint and a tomato plant that had grown taller than Bảo. Neighbours on the floor below began asking for seedlings, and a woman on the ninth floor now trades her spring onions for Bảo's mother's chillies.

Bảo has noticed that the balcony has changed more than their meals. His mother, who used to spend her evenings on her phone, now goes outside to check the plants. Bảo himself has started reading about which vegetables can grow well together. He still forgets to water the boxes sometimes, but he no longer thinks of a garden as something that needs a piece of ground.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Why vegetables from a balcony taste better than supermarket ones
How a family grew vegetables on a small balcony and what it changed
The problems of keeping snails away from a lettuce crop
A boy who learned to enjoy watering plants every morning
questions.explanation: The passage follows the balcony garden from three boxes to eleven, and ends with how it changed the family's habits. The taste, the snails and the watering are details along the way.

questions.q: Which of the first three crops was mostly lost?
options: The lettuce
The mint
The water spinach
The chillies
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says snails ate most of the lettuce and the rest turned bitter. The water spinach was a success, and the mint was only added later.

questions.q: Where did the chilli seeds come from?
options: From Bảo's school
From a market stall
From a neighbour on the ninth floor
From the family's kitchen
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the chilli seeds were ones his mother had saved from the kitchen. The market stall supplied the soil, not the seeds, and the neighbour trades spring onions.

questions.q: What can be inferred about the family's neighbours?
options: They were experienced gardeners before the family arrived
They have larger balconies than Bảo's family
They became interested in growing vegetables themselves
They complained about water dripping from the balcony
questions.explanation: Neighbours ask for seedlings and one woman swaps her own spring onions for chillies, which shows they have started growing things too. Nothing suggests complaints, experience or bigger balconies.

questions.q: The word "sowed" in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to:
options: watered
planted seeds of
cut
bought
questions.explanation: The sentence lists what went into each box: water spinach was planted, lettuce was sowed, chilli seeds went into the third. "Sow" means to put seeds in the soil.

questions.q: In paragraph 3, "the box" that was moved into the shade is:
options: the box of lettuce
the box of soil from the market
the box of water spinach
the box of chilli plants
questions.explanation: The sentences before describe the lettuce being eaten by snails and turning bitter in the afternoon heat, so moving it into the shade is the lesson the garden taught.

questions.q: Bảo's father was against the idea of growing vegetables in the flat.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: His father only pointed out that there was no garden and little sun. The passage does not say whether he opposed the idea or supported it.

passages.title: The Man at Number Seventeen
passages.passage:
When the house at number seventeen was finally sold last spring, everyone on our street was curious. It had stood empty for almost two years, and my younger brother Tí was sure a family with children would move in. Instead, a small van arrived one morning with an old man, a dog and about thirty boxes of books.

The man's name was Mr Tâm, and for the first month we hardly saw him. He did not come to the tea stall on the corner where the other neighbours gathered, and when my mother called good morning across the fence, he did not answer. Tí decided he was unfriendly. Mrs Hồng next door, who knows everything about everyone, said he had been a professor and probably thought he was too clever for us.

Everything changed on a rainy Tuesday in June. I was pushing my bicycle home with a broken chain when Mr Tâm's gate opened. He waved me in, turned the bicycle upside down on his porch and fixed the chain in five minutes without a word. Then he wrote something in a small notebook and held it up: "I hear very little. Please face me when you speak."

I felt terrible. We had all been talking about him for weeks, and he had not been able to hear a single one of our greetings. That evening I told my mother, and the next day she went to his gate with a plate of bánh xèo and a sheet of paper. Since then, the notebook has become a habit on our street. Tí has learned to tap Mr Tâm on the shoulder before speaking, and Mrs Hồng, to everyone's surprise, has stopped guessing and started asking.

Mr Tâm was indeed a professor, of engineering, and he now repairs bicycles for half the children in the neighbourhood. He refuses to take money, but he accepts cakes, and he says that he has never lived on a friendlier street.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: How a street misjudged a new neighbour before learning the truth about him
A retired professor who opens a bicycle repair shop
The problems that people with hearing loss face every day
Why a house stood empty for almost two years
questions.explanation: The story moves from the neighbours' wrong ideas about Mr Tâm to the discovery that he could not hear them, and how the street changed as a result. The repairs and the empty house are only details.

questions.q: Why did Mr Tâm not reply when the narrator's mother greeted him?
options: He was too busy unpacking his boxes of books
He could not hear her
He did not want to be disturbed by children
He thought he was too clever to talk to his neighbours
questions.explanation: His note explains it: I hear very little. The idea that he felt too clever for the street was only Mrs Hồng's guess, which turned out to be wrong.

questions.q: What can be inferred about Mrs Hồng?
options: She also has difficulty hearing
She had known Mr Tâm before he moved to the street
She tends to make up stories about people she does not know
She works at the tea stall on the corner
questions.explanation: She "knows everything about everyone" and decided Mr Tâm was a proud professor without speaking to him. The ending, where she stopped guessing and started asking, confirms this habit.

questions.q: The word "gathered" in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to:
options: sold tea
argued
waited for the bus
met together
questions.explanation: The tea stall is described as the place where the other neighbours gathered, that is, where they came together to talk.

questions.q: Why does the writer include the sentence "He refuses to take money, but he accepts cakes"?
options: To show that Mr Tâm is generous and has become part of the community
To suggest that Mr Tâm does not trust his neighbours
To show that Mr Tâm is poor and needs food
To explain why the children on the street like him
questions.explanation: Fixing bicycles for free and taking cakes instead shows a friendly exchange between Mr Tâm and the neighbours, which fits the final words about the friendliest street he has lived on.

questions.q: Mr Tâm had worked as a professor of engineering.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: The last paragraph confirms that he was indeed a professor, of engineering, so Mrs Hồng was right about his job even if wrong about his character.

questions.q: The house at number seventeen had been empty for more than three years.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says it had stood empty for almost two years, so the statement contradicts the passage.
